articles.title: Aaron Judge’s parents Patty and Wayne adopted him as a baby: How their love, guidance and support helped shape the NY Yankees captain’s life beyond MLB
articles.summary: Explore how Aaron Judge's upbringing by adoptive parents Patty and Wayne molded him into the New York Yankees captain he is today, highlighting values of hard work, humility, and family support in shaping his MLB career.
articles.body: Aaron Judge is best known for his towering home runs, his powerful presence and his leadership as captain of the New York Yankees. But his story is more than a baseball story and his upbringing has a lot to do with the person and the athlete he is today.Adopted by Patty and Wayne Judge the day after his birth, Aaron grew up in a family that stressed kindness, discipline, education and hard work. As he chased his baseball dreams and pursued his interests, his parents provided a supportive atmosphere that helped establish principles that still guide his life beyond Major League Baseball.How Aaron Judge was raised by Patty and Wayne JudgeAaron was adopted by Patty and Wayne Judge, and raised in Linden, California soon after his birth in April 1992. Both were teachers and their work backgrounds reflected the importance they placed on education, consistency and personal responsibility. Their style of parenting helped Aaron understand that being successful was about commitment, on and off the field.The Judges also spoke about Aaron’s older brother, John, who was also adopted. Aaron and his brother grew up in a family environment that valued family, support and shared experiences. His parents had instilled in him the value of hard work but to keep his feet on the ground, something that would serve him well as his baseball career unfolded.Aaron has publicly thanked Patty and Wayne for their part in his development. They supported him so that he could meet the rigors of competitive sports without losing the values he learned at home.How Aaron Judge’s family influenced his Yankees leadershipJudge’s leadership with the Yankees shows traits often associated with his upbringing: accountability, composure and respect for others. In December 2022, he was named team captain, a position that requires more than just making runs or hitting home runs. Captains are also expected to lead the way, support teammates and be a face of the organization.Those responsibilities were helped into place by the example of his parents. They taught discipline and humility, and that translated as Judge transitioned from playing amateur baseball to the major leagues, where the spotlight and expectations can be bright and heavy.And his family history also reminds us that an athlete’s development is not determined by statistics alone. Judge’s on-field accomplishments have earned him a place among baseball’s greats, but the man behind the public face is a product of years of nudging and mentoring away from the ballpark.Why the support of Patty and Wayne Judge still mattersJudge’s public musings on family and gratitude still have the weight of Patty and Wayne’s influence. In 2024, the couple was named the George and Barbara Bush Little League Parents of the Year, a recognition by Little League that highlighted their commitment to supporting Aaron’s growth and keeping the emphasis on character and not athletic prowess.They also influenced Judge’s approach to family life. In a 2026 interview with Esquire, he talked about the sacrifices his parents made to be at his games and school functions. He talked about the time they let him in and reminded him that it’s important to make people feel loved and included. He linked those experiences to how he wants to treat his own daughter and the people he encounters.The support of parents is the foundation of a successful baseball career, and then some, Judge says. His constant presence brought with it a sense of responsibility, perspective and appreciation for others. Those qualities still matter with him being a Yankee and a fan and building a life outside of professional baseball.His successes will be measured in records, awards and performances, but the values taught by Patty and Wayne provide another lens through which to see his journey, and their story shows how a supportive family can shape not just an elite athlete, but the man behind the uniform.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: New Aaron Judge Rumors Reveal Yankees Insiders Were 'Annoyed' By Star's Comments After Playoff Loss
articles.summary: The New York Yankees reportedly didn't appreciate Aaron Judge's public comments expecting the front office to go "all in" this offseason after the team yet again failed to win a World Series title.
articles.body:
The New York Yankees reportedly didn't appreciate Aaron Judge's public comments expecting the front office to go "all in" this offseason after the team yet again failed to win a World Series title.

According to Jon Heyman of the New York Post , "Sources say one or two Yankees [bigwigs] were slightly-to-somewhat annoyed that captain/three-time MVP Judge suggested the $320M Yankees could spend more after they were swept by the Rays in the division series. Yankees higher-ups will get over it because Judge has a great rapport with them. But they were said to be taken aback."

Judge made it pretty clear he expects the Yankees to make some changes over the winter after being swept out of the ALDS by the Tampa Bay Rays.

"We're the Yankees," he told reporters. "I feel like they should go all in and do what they need to do and find. If we've got holes, if it's finding certain players or personnel, whatever we need, you've got to go out there and get it. That's why I signed back here to play with the Yankees, to fight for a championship every single year, to go all in. That's what I do every offseason, get ready to give this team and this city everything I've got. So I expect them to do the same."

Judge was asked if he believed the Yankees have previously gone all in and somewhat sidestepped the question.

"It's tough to say," he told reporters. "I want to trade for everybody, sign everybody every single year, but I know that's not realistic. So they give us a winning team every single year, but that's not good enough here in New York. We're the Yankees. You've got to go out there and chase championships and go all in every year. So I'm excited to see what they do."

The Yankees had a $308.3 million payroll in 2026, the third-largest in baseball, so overall spending may not be an issue. How those funds are being allocated is another matter entirely.

The Yankees have a number of pending free agents, including infielder Jazz Chisholm Jr., outfielder Trent Grisham and closer David Bednar. Both Chisholm and Grisham took big steps back after excellent 2025 campaigns, though Bednar was excellent, finishing with 35 saves in 39 save opportunities.

And it may be time for an influx of new players anyway to mix up the current core around players like Judge. One way or another, he's expecting an aggressive offseason, even if the higher-ups seemingly would prefer if he didn't voice that desire publicly.

articles.title: Colin Cowherd's analogy of the 2026 Dodgers to The Godfather Part III is brilliant
articles.summary: Colin Cowherd compares the Los Angeles Dodgers' stunning 0-3 postseason hole to "The Godfather Part III" — familiar names, but fading magic.
articles.body: Perhaps the best analogy for the stunning 0-3 hole the Los Angeles Dodgers find themselves in comes from The Godfather – the third installment of the trilogy, that is. Credit FS1 host Colin Cowherd for the comparison Wednesday. "The Dodgers trying to win a third World Series is starting to have Godfather III vibes to it," he began. "Some of the names are familiar. Al Pacino. Diane Keaton. Francis Ford Coppola is still directing it. But it feels played. And the Dodgers feel played out." Brilliant. Now, for some ground rules before sharing the analogy widely. Before you start assigning Dodgers players to actors, understand that Pacino was still excellent in The Godfather Part III. Shohei Ohtani, universally recognized as the greatest baseball player in the world, has not been. Ohtani had batted under .200 in four straight postseason games. The Dodgers reportedly even considered benching him ahead of Game 3 because of his struggles and injuries. A DODGERS-LESS WORLD SERIES WOULD HURT NOW, BUT HELP MLB LATER | BOBBY BURACK But if the Dodgers don't somehow surge back from 0-3 and become just the second team in MLB history to overcome such a deficit in an LCS series, the Godfather analogy could hold up remarkably well. The Godfather and The Godfather Part II are two of the greatest films ever made. The opinion here is that the original is the greatest movie ever and the sequel – which is also partly a prequel – is somewhere in the top 10, maybe the top five. Part III isn't nearly as bad as some movie buffs sometimes portray it. However, it was undoubtedly a profound disappointment compared to the first two films. For one, Coppola cast his daughter Sofia as Mary Corleone. It didn't work. The romance between Mary and her first cousin Vincent consumed too much screen time for how little it ultimately contributed to the trilogy's conclusion. The absence of Tom Hagen is glaring, as is the loss of Sonny Corleone, whose death in the original film deprived the third installment of another defining character from the Corleone family. In sum, The Godfather trilogy would be remembered even more favorably had there never been a third film. There's a reason some Godfather marathons conveniently end after Part II. Likewise, if the Dodgers don't come back in this series, the 2026 team will be remembered as a stain on the legacy of the dynasty. Still, The Godfather Part III had excuses. The film was released 16 years after Part II. The principal cast had aged. Robert Duvall, who portrayed Hagen, did not return. And after nearly two decades, the first two films had been elevated to a standard that virtually no sequel could reasonably meet. The 2026 Dodgers have no such excuses. Their payroll exceeds that of the other three remaining teams combined. Los Angeles added Tarik Skubal and Kyle Tucker to a roster that was already considered one of the greatest ever assembled on paper. Granted, the cast, like in the film, is aging. They are trying to recapture old magic. It's not working. Nonetheless, we enjoyed the analogy. The Godfather Part III and the Dodgers' 2026 postseason are shaping up as two of the more memorable disappointments in their respective fields. Even depressed Dodgers superfan and OutKick reporter Ian Miller appreciated Cowherd's comparison. "There’s a case to be made that The Godfather Part 1 and Godfather Part 2 are two of the best movies ever made. Just like the 2024-2025 Dodgers are two of the best teams ever. If the price for that is getting pulled back in for the 2026 team, it was worth it," Miller said of Cowherd's analogy. articles.summary: Shohei Ohtani will be batting first when the Los Angeles Dodgers play Thursday night with their postseason on the line.
articles.body:
Shohei Ohtani will be batting first when the Los Angeles Dodgers play Thursday night with their postseason on the line.

Ohtani is back in the leadoff spot for Game 4 of the NLCS against the Milwaukee Brewers, according to the pregame lineup submitted by the Dodgers.

The Brewers are sticking with Jackson Chourio, Brice Turang and William Contreras at the top of the order while looking to win an NL pennant.

Mookie Betts batted first for the Dodgers in the first three games of the NLCS, during which the Brewers went 3-0 to put the two-time reigning champions on the brink of elimination.

The Dodgers' must-win Game 4 is set to start at 8 p.m. ET in Los Angeles.

Ohtani batted cleanup through the first two games of the NLCS and dropped to sixth in the lineup for Game 3.

Dodgers manager Dave Roberts told reporters he hadn't informed Ohtani he would be leading off Game 4 but instead "just posted the lineup."

"Just seeing the work the last couple of days, I like where he is head is at," Roberts said. "I liked the at-bats yesterday... obviously we haven't performed the way we are capable of, so kind of shake it up a little bit, but something that's of somewhat normalcy that our guys are used to."

Roberts continued, "I think that the work, being here til 9 o'clock two nights ago working, the at-bats yesterday— for me, baking all that in, I felt absolutely, put him at the top. I feel good about him taking five at-bats and giving us our best chance to win."

Ohtani has not been a regular at the top of the batting order since Sept. 2, the day before he revealed he was dealing with a right biceps issue in addition to a lingering left knee problem.

Those injuries have kept Ohtani from pitching since early July and contributed to limiting him to a .182 batting average with no home runs or RBIs in seven postseason games.

Roberts told The Athletic's Katie Woo and Ken Rosenthal he planned to have a conversation with Ohtani about potentially benching him for Game 3 of the NLCS.

Woo and Rosenthal reported at the time that rookie Josue De Paula was the top candidate to replace Ohtani should he be pulled from the lineup.

Ohtani ultimately stayed in the lineup Wednesday to record a hit and a walk in two at-bats during the Dodgers' 6-2 loss.

He will start out Thursday's game facing left-hander Shane Drohan, who will make his postseason debut when starting for the Brewers.

articles.summary: Petey Halpin's towering 385-foot two-run homer powered the Cleveland Guardians past the Tampa Bay Rays after weather moved the Game 3 start to 1 p.m. ET.

In the team's 3-2 loss to the Cleveland Guardians on Thursday at Progressive Field, the offense was dormant. The Rays scored just two runs on three hits, as the Guardians' pitching staff shut them down. In seven of the nine innings, the Rays went down in order. articles.title: Dodgers move Shohei Ohtani back to leadoff while facing NLCS elimination vs. Brewers
articles.summary: Ohtani has already batted second, fourth, fifth and sixth this postseason.
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have batted Shohei Ohtani second, fourth, fifth and sixth in their lineup across seven games this postseason. Now down 3-0 in the NLCS, they have one more idea for him.

Ohtani is batting leadoff in the Dodgers' batting order for Game 4 against the Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday, in which the club is attempting to begin a comeback from down 3-0 in the series.

Mookie Betts will move back to second, where he spent much of the regular season, with Freddie Freeman third and Will Smith in the clean-up spot.

Ohtani was the Dodgers' everyday leadoff hitter from June 2024 until September of this year. Due to struggles related to knee, biceps and neck issues, the Dodgers placed him on the injured list then tentatively put him in a leadoff platoon with Betts when he returned for the final five games of the season.

However, Ohtani has struggled mightily since coming back from the IL, resulting in him moving further back in the batting order until he was hitting sixth in Game 3 on Wednesday, his lowest placement since before his first MVP year in 2021 .

Ohtani, who has been adamant about continuing to play, did have a decent game on Wednesday, going 1-for-2 with a single, walk and hit-by-pitch. That was apparently enough to convince the Dodgers to give leadoff a try again.

Dodgers manager Dave Roberts' pregame explanation:

"Just seeing the work the last couple days, I like where his head is at. I like the at-bats yesterday and I felt that trying to shake it up a bit — obviously, we haven't performed the way that we're capable of. Something that's of somewhat normalcy that our guys are used to."

Ohtani still hasn't hit a home run since Aug. 18, but getting on base three out of four times at least bodes well for a more traditional leadoff man.

Ohtani's placement is ultimately a small button to press, but the Dodgers are at the point where they will try anything. Their offense, one of the best in baseball during the regular season, has gone dormant in the NLCS, if it already wasn't there in the NLDS against the Atlanta Braves.

Dodgers hitters are now 3-for-32 with runners in scoring position, with zero home runs this series. You can ascribe that to basic bad luck, a lack of execution from a veteran-heavy group, a clutch performance by the Brewers (and Braves) pitchers or some sort of Space Jam-esque talent robbery, but it all adds up to a unit that needs a change.

Game 4 is scheduled for Thursday at 5 p.m. PT at Dodger Stadium (Fox Sports 1).

articles.title: Want to know how to win in October? The 2026 Milwaukee Brewers are providing the blueprint
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers lead the Dodgers 3-0 in the NLCS despite more strikeouts, proving Major League Baseball playoffs have no secret formula.
articles.body: It's arguably the most important question for organizations and fans across Major League Baseball; how do you win in the playoffs? There's a theoretical formula for getting to October, draft and develop well, build a complete roster that has depth at key positions, use analytics to piece together the best mix of skill sets and sign targeted free agents to fill in missing pieces. The more money you have, the easier it is to sign those free agents, of course, but as the Yankees, Mets, Giants, and Angels will tell you, playing in a big market and acquiring expensive talent doesn't always guarantee results. But once you're in the postseason, how can you ensure your team gets a spot in the World Series? The ultimate goal, the only outcome that matters, and the only determinant of the "best team in baseball?" A DODGERS-LESS WORLD SERIES WOULD HURT NOW, BUT HELP MLB LATER | BOBBY BURACK The 2026 Milwaukee Brewers are showing the rest of the sport exactly how it's done. For context, the Brewers enter Thursday afternoon as overwhelming favorites to advance to the World Series thanks to their 3-0 series lead over the Los Angeles Dodgers. The Dodgers have the most expensive roster in the sport, though by active player payroll in 2026 they did trail the New York Mets, depending on which source you use. Milwaukee? They were just 19th this season. They traded away Freddy Peralta, their best pitcher, in 2025, a year after trading star closer Devin Williams to the Yankees, and trading Corbin Burnes to the Baltimore Orioles. Their big offseason acquisitions were backup catcher Gary Sanchez, Angel Zerpa, Jake Woodford, and a trade to bring in David Hamilton, Shane Drohan and Kyle Harrison from the Boston Red Sox for infielder Caleb Durbin and a few other players. During the season, their big moves were watching Tarik Skubal go to the Dodgers, getting Dustin May and JoJo Romero, and adding reliever Antonio Senzatela. If that sounds underwhelming, it's because it is. Yet in game one of the NLCS, the Brewers beat Skubal 2-1. In game two, they came roaring back from deficit after deficit, knocking out World Series hero Yoshinobu Yamamoto on their way to an easy 7-4 win. In game three, they fell behind late, only to score five straight runs and cruise to yet another 6-2 win. So how are they doing it? They've found the blueprint. Milwaukee, we've been told by very experienced baseball analysts, is winning because they don't strike out. Their approach is based on contact. Put the ball in play, the thinking goes, don't just try and hit home runs. These analysts have decades of experience at the highest level of baseball. Obviously, they'd have enormous insight and detailed statistical breakdowns backing up their opinions. Well, in game one of the NLCS, the Dodgers struck out eight times, meaning they put the ball in play on 23 of their 31 at bats. Milwaukee struck out 13 times, only putting the ball in play in 13 of their 26 at bats. So the Dodgers' home run approach resulted in...fewer strikeouts and more balls put in play. 10 more balls put in play, in fact, a massive number in just one game. But the Brewers won anyway, 2-1. Interesting. In game two of the NLCS, the Dodgers struck out nine times, while Milwaukee struck out 10. Funnily enough, the only home run was hit by William Contreras for the Brewers. They won 7-4. In game three, Milwaukee struck out a whopping 12 times in 35 at bats against Blake Snell and the Dodgers bullpen. Los Angeles? Their hitters had just eight strikeouts in 32 at bats. The Dodgers put the ball in play 24 times, Milwaukee did 23 times. Yet the Brewers won 6-2 anyway. How? Because they hit three home runs, while Los Angeles yet again put up a goose egg. So in three games, the Brewers have struck out 35 times, averaging nearly 12 per game. The Dodgers have struck out 25 times, or just over eight per game. That's so odd because all the baseball analysts have been saying that Milwaukee's superior approach, just putting the ball in play, getting the bat on the ball, is the reason they're winning. Yet they're making contact far less often than the Dodgers are, with their awful, new school, analytics-driven, home run-only offense. And Milwaukee has a 5-0 home run advantage in a series they're winning three games to none. Wonder what that means. We'll come back to that, but what about the contact itself? Maybe the Brewers have instructed their hitters to purposefully hit the ball poorly, while the Dodgers hitting staff keeps telling Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts, and Shohei Ohtani to hit the ball hard directly at Milwaukee defensive players. Obviously, weak contact is preferable to hitting the ball hard, because that's old school baseball or something. Here's what one user, "Dubs Only Sports" found in a post made on X. Headlined "luck doesn't exist in baseball," which is obviously true because every single outcome is the result of purposeful decision making while randomness is just a fake conspiracy theory, they found that, shockingly enough, there's been little difference in quality of contact between the two teams. But a tremendous difference in outcomes. The Dodgers have 29 hard hit balls in the series, defined as being hit at 95 mph or above. Those 29 hard-hit balls have resulted in 12 hits and no home runs. Milwaukee has just 21 hard hit balls in the series, which have resulted in 11 hits and five home runs. Well sure, you might say, but who cares about hard-hit balls when you can just hit the ball poorly and steer it in the right direction? Turns out, the Dodgers are trying that too! LA has 40 balls put in play this series that were "soft contact," or under 95 mph. On those 40 balls put in play, they've gotten just three hits, good for a .075 batting average. Milwaukee has put 42 balls in play with soft contact, resulting in 16 hits and a .381 batting average. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Wow! So the Dodgers are more frequently hitting the ball harder, and putting nearly as many weakly hit balls into play, a difference of less than one per game, than Milwaukee. They're striking out far less often than the Brewers. Yet their results have been much worse. Really makes you think, doesn't it? In actuality, of course, it will not make anyone think, because of the inescapable conclusion: nothing actually matters. Sarcasm aside, that's the real answer to the "secret formula" for winning in October: there is no secret formula. Just be a pretty good team and hope you get the benefit of timing with your offense and pitching staff. When it comes to postseason baseball, the gaps between teams are so small that the win probability for each team is only marginally different from a coin flip. Per FanGraphs baseball analyst Dan Szymborski, creator of the ZiPS projection system, the Dodgers had a 58% chance of winning the series before it started. That's what a $250 million payroll gap buys, a 58% chance instead of a 50% chance. Obviously, the outcome in this year's NLCS is the 42%. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Because the gaps are so small, as opposed to sports with poor competitive balance like the NFL, the outcomes rely much more heavily on luck and random chance that fans or very smart analysts will ever admit. Because humans have to have an explanation for everything, every result is ascribed to some kind of intent, process, or approach, as opposed to the inherent variability of baseball. Milwaukee's bullpen has allowed two runs in around 32 innings in the postseason. Filled with castoffs from other teams and cheap internal options having the best few weeks of their careers at the perfect time. That's not unexpected or unusual, it's an undeniable part of baseball. Their batting average on balls in play in this NLCS is .393, where league average is around .300. The Dodgers? Just .221. Milwaukee has a 31.3% strikeout rate, while the Dodgers' is just 23.4%. Milwaukee has outperformed their expected stats, based on quality of contact, by nearly 20 points. The Dodgers have underperformed by 67 points. The Brewers aren't winning because of soft contact, they're winning because they've hit home runs and benefitted from fortunate bounces on balls put in play. This isn't to say that the Brewers aren't a good team, because of course they are. They somehow managed to turn Jake Bauers from an unplayable castoff, to a top-10 hitter in baseball. Misiorowski is the likely NL Cy Young Award winner. Their prospects, like Brice Turang, Jackson Chourio and Garrett Mitchell have all panned out, a testament to their player development staff. Every single trade they've made in recent years has worked out in their favor, another feather in the cap for their scouting department. But the Brewers have inarguably gotten "lucky" this series, because the results have outperformed the quality of their contact and approach. The Dodgers got lucky to win in 2024 and 2025. Luck is not a byproduct in postseason baseball, it is quite literally required. Over a large enough sample size, most of the randomness and luck in baseball evens out. Meaning that if the Dodgers played the Brewers 162 times, LA's talent advantage would almost certainly matter, to the point where they would win 58% of the games. But in a best-of-seven? Or a best-of-five? The talent advantage is so small that a few bounces either way can lead to a wildly different outcome. Which is what we're seeing. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER This is why the guiding philosophy in baseball has become, "do what you can to win 85 games and hope for the best." Because that gives you a 42% chance of beating the most talented roster in a playoff series. It's rational, because it's correct. The Toronto Blue Jays rode Addison Barger and Ernie Clement to within two outs of a championship. They finished in last place this year. OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD LA's success in 2024 and 2025 has given fans the inaccurate impression that World Series results are a foregone conclusion, when the exact opposite is true. The Dodgers have made the postseason 17 times since 2008. When they're eliminated by Milwaukee this week, they'll have won three championships in 17 tries. There is no sport less predictable than baseball. There is no way to "ruin" baseball, or to break it, or to build unbeatable superteams. Because the volatility of it will create series with outcomes like this, where the Dodgers hit the ball harder, make more contact, strike out less, and still get obliterated. Even if LA put together a roster with Skubal, Yamamoto, Paul Skenes, Misiorowski, Aaron Judge, Ohtani, Bobby Witt Jr., Freddie Freeman, Junior Caminero, and Pete Crow-Armstrong, that team would have a 58-60% chance of winning a best-of-seven postseason series against the 84-win Cleveland Guardians. It doesn't sound right, but it is objective fact. Looking for meaning in October is pointless. Looking for a blueprint of how to win the World Series is insanity.

articles.title: Petey Halpin becomes the Guardians' latest unlikely hero with the big swing to take ALCS Game 3 over the Rays
articles.summary: The 24-year-old Halpin has been a surprising late addition to a Guardians season already defined by impact rookies.
articles.body:
CLEVELAND — The first time Petey Halpin played at Progressive Field, the ballpark was practically empty. Little did he know that one day, that same ballpark would be jam-packed and chanting his name in October.

Exactly 2,659 days before Halpin launched a go-ahead, two-run homer to help the Cleveland Guardians inch closer to the World Series with a 3-2 victory on Thursday in ALCS Game 3 , he was a talented teenager chasing his big-league dreams. He had just turned 17 and was invited to play in MLB's High School All-Star Game leading up to the Midsummer Classic in Cleveland in 2019. While the big-league club was across the state taking on the Reds, 40 of the best prep prospects in the country gathered on Cleveland's home turf to play a seven-inning scrimmage in front of scattered groups of friends and family, plus a contingent of amateur scouts. The outfield seats and upper decks were entirely unoccupied.

That was certainly not the case Thursday, when 30,101 fans packed Progressive Field for Game 3 between the Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays. The two clubs split the first two games at Tropicana Field before the series shifted to Ohio, where the weather forecast loomed large. Projected rain for Thursday evening prompted MLB to move first pitch up to 1 p.m., making it harder for fans to fill the stadium on a weekday afternoon. But with the rain still hours away, Game 3 unfolded in picturesque postseason conditions — 62 degrees and sunny — and the crowd was buzzing. It was an ideal stage for another memorable October chapter for the Guardians, with Halpin at the center of it.

In the second inning, Nathaniel Lowe gave the Guardians a 1-0 lead with an RBI double. Cleveland starter Gavin Williams picked up where he left off from his spectacular ALDS performance, cruising through three perfect innings on 35 pitches with five strikeouts. But the Rays broke through in the fourth, when the speedy Chandler Simpson smoked a triple down the right-field line to drive in Yandy Díaz and Victor Mesa Jr. and make it 2-1 Tampa Bay.

With the bottom third of Cleveland's order due up in the fifth, Rays relievers Cam Booser and Tyler Wells started warming in the bullpen while starter Griffin Jax sought to collect a few more outs. But Patrick Bailey led off with an infield single, bringing the rookie Halpin to the plate as the go-ahead run. In a 2-2 count, Jax attacked with a sinker right down the middle. Halpin didn't miss; his left-handed swing connected with authority. The ball jumped off his bat at 105 mph and soared toward the right-center-field seats.

On contact, it looked like a no-doubter, and Halpin reacted as such, admiring the ball's trajectory as he slowly walked sideways toward first base. The wind was blowing hard toward home plate, however, putting the ball's final destination momentarily in doubt. But Halpin hit it well enough. The ball landed just over the wall, and pandemonium ensued. Halpin flipped his bat nearly 10 feet straight up over his head and began the biggest home run trot of his life.

"I definitely threw it high," Halpin conceded postgame. "I think just the moment and that being for sure the biggest moment of my career, just the energy and the excitement — just kind of let it go."

"Ten out of 10," reliever Daniel Espino rated Halpin's bat flip afterward. "I thought it was going to hit him in the head on the way down."

"He smashed that," fellow rookie Travis Bazzana said. "I was like, that's a no-doubter — it's way gone. But the wind was howling right into that ball, so it kind of snuck out. But it deserved to be a homer, that's for sure."

That concluded the scoring in Game 3. Both bullpens breezed through the remainder of the contest unblemished, with Cleveland closer Cade Smith notching the final four outs to seal the one-run victory. Besides Simpson's three-bagger, it was a brutal day for Tampa Bay's bats, most notably Junior Caminero, who went 0-for-4 with four strikeouts for just the second time in his career.

The Game 3 hero, Halpin, 24, has been a surprising late addition to a Guardians season already defined by impact rookies such as Parker Messick, Chase DeLauter and Bazzana. After spending most of the season's first half in Triple-A, Halpin's plus speed and defense in center field earned him more consistent playing time down the stretch, though his offensive contributions were fleeting.

But in September, he delivered one of the biggest hits of the Guardians' season as Cleveland chased down another division title: a dramatic, go-ahead home run against the Chicago White Sox, an ultra-rare spark of success for Halpin against a southpaw. And when Angel Martínez slumped to begin the postseason, manager Stephen Vogt inserted Halpin into the starting lineup at the end of the ALDS, hoping his high-energy style could make a difference. On Thursday, Halpin's big swing — and even bigger bat flip — delivered exactly that.

"I'm really happy for Petey," Vogt said. "It's the second time he's kind of picked us up in a big spot this year and a really fun moment for him — great swing."

When Halpin took the field in Cleveland as a 17-year-old, his performance was fairly forgettable. The stakes were low, the attendance even lower. Now that same venue is chanting "Petey! Petey!" as he tries to do his part to push Cleveland closer to ending the longest World Series drought in the major leagues.

After his big swing on Thursday, the home team needs just two more wins to advance to the Fall Classic — and with two more home games on deck, they'll have the crowd behind them.

"Just having as much momentum as we can possibly have, and being able to feed off of that, feed off the crowd, feed off the energy," he said. "It's a lot of fun."

articles.title: New Yankees Rumors Update Jazz Chisholm Jr, Bednar Qualifying Offer Buzz Ahead of MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: The New York Yankees could reportedly be considering allowing second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. to hit free agency this offseason.
articles.body:
The New York Yankees could reportedly be considering allowing second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. to hit free agency this offseason.

The New York Post 's Jon Heyman reported Thursday the Yankees are expected to extend a qualifying offer to closer David Bednar but are "unlikely" to make the same offer to Chisholm.

The Post 's Joel Sherman previously reported the qualifying offer for the 2027 season will be $23.15 million.

Bednar, 32, recorded a 2.47 ERA and 1.038 WHIP through 69.1 innings across 64 relief appearances this season. Chisholm, 28, batted .231 with 19 home runs, 55 RBI and 41 stolen bases in 137 games.

Chisholm is one year removed from becoming the third player in Yankees history to record 30 home runs and 30 stolen bases in a single season.

The following campaign ended with a postseason marred by defensive errors that led to Chisholm getting pulled from the starting lineup for Games 1 and 3 of the ALDS.

He expressed discontentment with Yankees manager Aaron Boone for not informing Chisholm ahead of time he would be replaced by Anthony Volpe in the Game 3 starting lineup.

When asked about his future with the Yankees after the Tampa Bay Rays completed their series sweep in Game 3, Chisholm still indicated he was interested in returning to the Bronx.

Bednar made three appearances during the postseason, allowing a hit and a walk but no runs in his three innings on the mound.

Keeping him in the Bronx would mark the first time in years the Yankees have committed significant money to their bullpen.

The Yankees haven't had a reliever make more than Bednar's 2026 season of $9 million since Aroldis Chapman and Zack Britton in 2022, per Spotrac .

Eight other Yankees players are heading into the offseason as pending free agents . The list most notably also includes Trent Grisham, who signed a qualifying offer to stay with the Yankees last season, alongside Paul Blackburn and Paul Goldschmidt.

Any qualifying offers to eligible players must be issued by the fifth day after the World Series. The Yankees could receive draft compensation should any players receive qualifying offers but sign with other teams.

articles.title: Royals Star Named Finalist for Award Voted On by His Peers
articles.summary: Bobby Witt Jr. is up for one of baseball's top player-voted honors after a strong year in a losing season.
articles.body:
The players who had to face shortstop Bobby Witt Jr. all summer still think he was one of the best in the American League, even in a rough year for the Kansas City Royals .

The MLB Players Association announced its finalists for the 2026 Players Choice Awards on Wednesday, and Witt is one of three players up for the AL Outstanding Player Award.

His competition is designated hitter Yordan Álvarez of the Houston Astros and third baseman Junior Caminero of the Tampa Bay Rays, with the winners set to be announced the week of Oct. 26.

The players vote on these awards themselves, and the union said the voting took place in September with help from the accounting firm KPMG.

This nod is a little different from the other honors Witt has picked up this fall because it comes from the guys who faced him every night instead of from writers or coaches.

Witt was already named a finalist for the Hank Aaron Award , and on Wednesday he was also named a Gold Glove finalist at shortstop after winning the AL award at that spot in each of the last two years.

Over 143 games, he hit .281 with a .359 on-base percentage, 18 home runs, 45 stolen bases and 94 runs scored.

He made the All-Star team, and Baseball-Reference credits him with 6.7 WAR despite a stint on the injured list with low back tightness in late July.

All of that came on a Kansas City team that finished 69-93 and last in the AL Central.

When Witt spoke with FanSided late in the season , he did not hide how let down he was, and he took some of the blame himself.

"It's one of those things where you learn a lot about who you are individually and how you can become better. I feel like that's something to take away from this year," Witt said.

He also said the team got away from playing good baseball and has to get back to doing the little things.

Witt admitted the club needs more pieces as well, and the record backs him up.

I like hearing that from the face of the franchise, because Witt could have pointed at the injuries or the bullpen and instead talked about getting better himself.

I am not sure he beats out Álvarez or Caminero, but getting picked by his peers while playing for a 93-loss team shows how much respect Witt has earned around the league.

Catcher Carter Jensen did not get the same treatment, even after hitting 27 home runs with 81 RBIs and being picked as the top rookie catcher by MLB Pipeline , since he was left out of the three-man AL rookie group.

That shows how hard it is to get noticed on a losing team.

Kansas City has a young core to build around with Witt and Jensen at the front of it.

My guess is that Witt has a better shot at a third straight Gold Glove than at this award, but making this list at all after a 69-93 year is a credit to how he played.
